Hero Siege has always been a game with an identity crisis. I bought this game way back when it was a rogue-lite, not an arpg/hack-n-slash. Back then there were no items, only relics as rogue-likes tend to have. It was enjoyable. 

But then one day they decided to turn it into an arpg and slowly did. For the most part they copied mechanics from Diablo 3 with no rhyme nor reason behind it. No one really cared if the mechanics were good, or if they even worked in the first place in Diablo 3, as long as D3 did it, Hero Siege copied.

Ironically enough, Hero Siege managed to become a better game than D3 ever was despite being a pixel graphics copy cat. I'd say the game peaked a couple years ago when it first introduced its auction house and made trading way easier. However the bad part about peaking is that its all downhill from there. In the patches since things kept getting reworked with no clear end goal, mechanics kept getting more and more convoluted after each and every rework. The way heroes scaled changed completely several times with no gain whatsoever and eventually the mythical HS2.0 was announced.

And boy is it here.

Remember all those d3 mechanics that were copied? Gone, to ashes. They were no longer "good enough". The new ideas? Copy Diablo 2. I shit you not. This game went from brainlessly copying 1 diablo game to another.

Why in the year of 2023 we are copying ideas and mechanics that were made with the consideration of the limitations of computers from the 1990s, or the lack of online guides/forums, is beyond me. 

[list]
    [*]Why are runewords in the game? The original goal of runewords was the be sort of an easter egg for a borderline "pre-internet" era. This shit is completely pointless in today's world
    [*]Why are we copying small potions from diablo 2? I dont know a single person who thinks potion spamming is good game design. It was something they went with 25 years ago. It was bad then and its bad now. The difference is, back then it was trying something new, now its a fucking joke.
    [*]Why are we copying a 20 year old UI from D2? Setting skills used to be simple. You click on skill slot, you choose which skill you want there. Now you click on the 1 skill slot you have, and then have to hover over the skill, click your, hidden by default, keybind for addition skills and now you have that skill keybinded, just like diablo 2 did 20 years ago. Just fucking why?
    [*]Why are we copying charms? Yes this game copied Diablo 2 charms with diablo 2's inventory. Fucking why? Again, this was trying new things 20 years ago, its a fucking joke now.
[/list]

In the end, in the last piece of greatest irony, by getting rid of the things it copied from d3, this game managed to become just as unplayable of a mess as d3 is.

People complaining that they "removed" expansions seem to be completely unaware that they are part of the base game now, and are found in the same place as they always were:
• Karp of Doom was Act 5, and is still Act 5.
• Depths of Hell was Act 6, and is still Act 6.
• Wrath of Mevis was Act 7, and is still Act 7.
Any Collectors Edition content (which is cosmetic) is STILL there, tied to your account... and is now exclusive to people who bought it before they rolled the expansions into the main game.

As for "never needing to log in", the log in is only for online play, and has ALWAYS been required for online play. You can still play offline as you have always been able to.

The game did go through a pretty major shift in game play mechanics...
It was previously a 'rogue lite' Diablo clone with almost platformer like mechanics -- You would collect up to 30 relics that provided various boosts and abilities, typically obtained from chests at the end of a jumping puzzle/challenge. When you died, even in "softcore", you lost all of your relics and needed to start over again.
Now the game is a more traditional Diablo-clone but with the jump mechanics retained. You no longer lose your relics on death, but are limited to 4 (which you can level up by collecting copies).

It would have been nice if they kept the original game as a separate mode offline, but the devs are a small studio and honestly the game has enough interface bugs/issues as-is.

I would´ve recommended this game, but there are some serious issues that can´t and won´t be fixed by the devs. 
But before I list my [u]Positive and Negative Aspects of the game[/u], let´s just find out what Hero Siege is about


[h1]What is Hero Siege?[/h1]

Hero Siege is a Top-down Diablo-like RPG Hack and Slash with some kind of Rogue-like elements in it.
There are a total of 17 Classes of which 8 are free to choose from, the other 9 classes are locked behind a paywall.
You start your journey as a level 1 Character and play through 6 Acts, each Act has 4 "normal" stages with the 5th being the Boss Stage that houses the Act-Boss. 
To reach the next stage you have to kill a certain amount of enemies, in order to spawn a stage Boss which you have to defeat to further progress. 
Each stage is randomly generated. After completing Act 6 you unlock the next difficulty, there are a total of 4 difficulties starting with "Normal", "Nightmare", "Hell" and "Inferno".

During your journey you will gather:
[list]
[*]EXP/Levels/Talent Points [spoiler]Level 100 is the maximum so you have 100 Talent Points to level up your favorite Skills, each capping at 30 Talent Points[/spoiler]
[*]Gold [spoiler]used for buying Keys to open Chests/Wormholes[/spoiler]
[*]Equipment with diverse rarity-levels [spoiler]"Normal", "Rare", "Legendary", "Mythic", "Satanic" and "Satanic-Set" and "Angelic") [u]NOTE:[/u] Satanic and Satanic-Set, as well as Angelic only drop in difficulty "Hell" and "Inferno"[/spoiler]
[*]Rubies [spoiler]used to buy ingame cosmetics and Satanic Items from other players, rubies are also used to level up your Satanic Items[/spoiler]
[*]Relics [spoiler]Buff-Items that make you stronger, giving you certain procc-chances or even enable you to fly, you can have a maximum of 31 of these - upon death you will lose every single one of your acquired relics but they can be found again[/spoiler]
[/list]

But why play this game, what´s the endgame? Your goal in this game is to reach Character Level 100 and unlock "Inferno" Difficulty. After hitting Character Level 100 you gain Paragon-like Levels that increase your choice of Stats by the factor +1%.
The ultimative challenge in this game are the "Wormholes" Portals that can be opend via a key that can be bought from NPCs with Gold. There are Leaderboards for how far every Class made progress in Wormholes, Solo, Duo, Trio and Squad Ranking.

[*]The In-Game Community is nice to newbies

Run the game in BETA mode (Set in game properties in steam), switch back to main game mode after running once in BETA mode and the error will now be gone.

1) Right click game in steam and select properties
2) Go to BETA tab on the properties window
3) Select the drop down (Select the beta..) and change from none, to openbeta.
4) Launch game and when in the menus, you can exit out. 
5) Repeat step 1., 2. and 3. but this time change the drop down back to the orignal value - from openbeta to none
6) Launch game and the problem should be resolved

This game used to be a lot of fun. Back in Season 1, it had a simple but addictive loop — kill enemies, collect artifacts with cool effects, and speedrun through waves before starting fresh on the next run. It was fast, satisfying, and genuinely unique.

It originally felt like a game in the spirit of The Binding of Isaac — simple, replayable, and full of cool item synergies. But now, it looks and plays more like a cheap Diablo knockoff. They could’ve just kept the original gameplay loop, added multiplayer, and expanded the artifact system with more item combos. Instead, they completely changed the formula, adding clunky ARPG mechanics and pay-to-play systems that ruined what made the original so fun.

Now it’s a completely different game. It barely resembles what I originally bought. The core gameplay that made it special is gone, and there’s no way to revert to earlier builds or replay the classic version. Honestly, it feels like false advertising at this point.

What we have now isn’t the game I paid for — it’s bloated, paywalled garbage. The developer clearly doesn’t listen to the community, and instead of gutting the old version, they should’ve just made Hero Siege 2 instead.

I wouldn’t recommend anyone buy this game in its current state. Spend your money on something like The Binding of Isaac or Heroes of Hammerwatch — you’ll have a much better time and be supporting developers who actually care about their players.

I'm writing this review from the perspective of someone who mainly plays the game solo, and occasionally with friends in Softcore Trade. 

Some context beforehand which I think is important:

The game has suffered from a wave of negative reviews dating back to its old roguelike days and it has since evolved  into an ARPG as we know it (PoE, Diablo, Grim Dawn etc), so a lot of those reviews no longer reflect its current state.

Performance:
Runs surprisingly well on Linux as a native client, which is a huge plus for me and it should be the same for Steam Deck users. General performance has improved over time, although multiplayer can still struggle and even see single digit FPS when the party is full and enemies aren't getting one shot.

Gameplay and Build Variety:
* A huge roster of classes gives plenty of replayability and diversity in gameplay
* Itemization feels heavily inspired by Diablo 2 and this is including rarity and drop rates
* If you enjoy long-term grinding and incremental upgrades, this is the one

That said, balance is nonexistent, which is understandable given the small development team but still very noticeable. Some classes have such an easy way into the endgame, while others can be a real struggle to get up and running.

Loot and Progression:

* Loot chase is satisfying, but it can feel punishing solo compared to group farming
* SSF (named Odyssey in here) mode offers a 30% loot increase, which should be the standard for all aRPGs
* The loot filter is excellent, intuitive and very easy to customize to your liking

A side note:
Drops are now server-side authenticated and the in-game economy seems stable (about 2 weeks into the current season), which wasn't the case before this season and has improved the trade experience immensely. 

Graphics:
* The retro art style is charming and gives off strong old school jRPG vibes
* Performance overall is improving, though again group play is in dire need of optimization

Some Downsides:
* Tooltips can be unclear (though they’ve been improving recently)
* Solo players may find the grind discouraging

Final Thoughts for now:

If you're looking for a Diablo 2–style loot grinder with tons of classes and long-term farming, this game is worth your time. It's not perfect by any means, but it's been improving over time.

Pros : Art, Simplicity in game-play, Ability to play together with friends
Cos : Locked classes, Loot unable to be equipped promoting micro transactions, Poor balancing on abilities as they get levelled up, Bugs, Inability to play characters in both online and offline mode, Inhospitable discord server. 

The game is pretty straightforward and chill. The pixel art is pretty and you can play it with your favourite music on or with your friends. The game is super easy, no tutorial needed. 

 You choose your class which comes with different abilities and 2 skill trees, from which you can choose the abilities you prefer to level up. From all classes you only get a few free classes to try out, i believe 4. The big majority of the classes in game need to be separately bought to be unlocked. You then kill enemies and get better equipment as you get to higher difficulty levels. As you level up your stats get automatically increased and you get 1 point per level to distribute to one of your abilities on any of the 2 ability trees for your character. As you increase the difficulty, you get a higher chance of rarer equipment or weapon drops. 

 However there is always the possibility the said rarest drop you will get, or many of them to be locked to a specific class. Actually since the majority of classes aren't free to play when purchasing the game most of the best items you will get you won't be able to use even if you wish to pass them on to a new character you will make from another class, unless you give in and buy the character for the class locked item you just got. 

 In the beginning you feel how unique of a character you can create with so many options to choose from and the limited points you get (100 is the limit once you reach level 100). In the early stages you need to go down your ability tree to unlock different abilities while you always get 1 main damage ability at least. You can reset your abilities at any point. You have 4 active abilities per class to use at a time. Since you have 2 ability trees to pick and match abilities along with all the passive abilities which are even more, you get a sense of control and fun in creating your own character. Unfortunately as you level up your character your first active abilities become less and less effective and you have to rely on (1 or both of) the last damaging abilities in your ability trees unless you want to take forever to grind your way to the next level. It's not a viable choice to put points in the early abilities because they level up so poorly as you put more points in them. It would be so interesting to be able to play around with the abilities you enjoy using, instead of having the facade of having an option when the first damaging maxed out ability with all 20 points added does half the damage of the last damaging ability with only 1 point added to it.

 Apart from this there are bugs that can break the game and ruin your fun. For example here are a few of the ones I encountered: gates in dungeons that are closed which should have been open, enemies stuck and not moving, enemies running outside of the reachable map making the player unable to finish a dungeon or the Chaos Tower, a bug where enemies 1 shot you. As for the way to report bugs, they could have made it way simpler.

 As a casual player i would normally recommend this if you wish to play it while travelling, on a ship for example and have no internet connection to pass your time or with friends online. Sadly you can't do both with the same character. If you want to be able to play with your friends you need to make an online character. If you wish to play offline you need to make a local character. So basically you are unable to play with friends with the same character you play with while offline. It would be much better if you could do both. 

 Their community discord has a small player base there. Even so some of the moderators are so unwilling to help out that is baffling. They can be rude and give off the impression they don't want to deal with any issues or newcomers which makes the place inhospitable. 

 All in all, I do enjoy it sometimes while i do other stuff in the meantime. It's a silly time waster but i wouldn't recommend it to my friends until some of these issues are dealt with.

[i]Hero Siege[/i] is like [i]Diablo[/i] stripped to its core, with some [i]The Binding of Isaac[/i]-like rogue elements added as spices. It's a top-down action hack 'n slash with 16-bit graphics, to be played as one of seven distinct characters, each with their own abilities and skills. During one's walk around the arena, there's gold and (some) loot to be picked up, there are (many) monsters to be slain, and every six levels, a boss (some amazingly easy, some excruciatingly difficult) awaits you. Levels and enemies are random-generated from a relatively large numer of possibilities, which guarentees a lot of differentiation. There are - very Diablo-like.. - several chapters, each chapter having 30 (!!) levels. So far, so good: the idea is sound, the graphics are fun although a bit blurred, and the gameplay - if using an Xbox 360-like controller - is as fluid as one could hope for.

But [i]Hero Siege[/i] also has its share of problems. The "rpg-light"-like leveling system, with stats- and skill-points to be distributed as one levels up, is way too unbalanced. Stats go only up by fractions of percentages, making it fairly useless to upgrade them, except maybe from level 50 or so on. Action skills are sometimes VERY powerful after a time, which will be necessary - but some are really over-the-top. Opposed to this, the amount of damage one can get while playing, is completely unpredictable. This is by itself a good thing, but some bullet-firing skulls deal such an amount of damage, that during the first six levels at least, you can die in an instant without even knowing what hit you. The graphics tend to hide these skulls sometimes, and that makes it really frustrating. It's not funny to get killed out-of-the-blue without even having a hint of what hit you. Though I have to admit, once at a certain level (certainly from 31 upwards), these devils can be survived better. Power-ups, dropped by the bosses, are really essential to survive for a longer time - but since they drop randomly as well, some games are fun because of the great assets they give, others are really disappointing since you didn't get anything worthwhile for a long time.

The good thing is that the developers are still finetuning things, and taking comments from the community into consideration, as far as I can see. That's why I give this game a thumbs-up, even if I've cried out sometimes in frustration when my poor newly-made marksman got out of the blue hit once more by a deadly bullet. What should really be implemented is a better save system: relics (power-ups) tend to get lost once I quit the game, and saving is actually only possible every act (30 levels).
This game has potential, is strangely addictive (although the 152 (!!!) Steam achievements seem like impossible to get), but still has serious flaws. Luckily, the developers are still finetuning and working on it.

UPDATE (08/15)

Being curious about how the game looks and plays now, almost I year later, I started it up again, to find out some things have been improved indeed. The levelling system seems much more balanced now, there are new chapters & classes and the overall feel is more polished. However, once in-game I quickly stumbled upon the "old problems": some enemies/bullets can still kill you instantly, and since you can't always see them coming through the mayhem this really is bothering. Overall though, I find the game to have improved significantly over the past year.
The large amount of achievements has been turned down a notch or two, so that it's easier to get a reasonable number of achievements overall.

[b]Conclusion: recommended, but not for the casual gamer looking for some easy fun[/b]

[h1]Multi player[/h1]

OK, so this is the part that, after many hours in-game and countless patches released by developers, made me write this review.

Long story short: I bought the game mid-June 2015, noticing a fun indie title with overwhelmingly positive (back then) reviews. Well, fuck me, I bought a 4-pack to play with friends, bought the DLCs, told friends to buy DLCs (or bought them myself then gifted) so we can play the whole thing together, that sort of thing - you know the drill. Tried playing - nope, had to portforward, as peer-to-peer wasn't available back then. OK, no big deal, added one rule to firewall and all is good. Tried again - massive synchronisation problems, invisible monsters, traps working out of sync from the server. Game was basically unplayable, because it seemed like each player was seeing different game. So the game was shelved, hoping that errors will be patched, network protocol will be fixed and so on.

Fast-forward to 2016: things are unbelievably and utterly shitty. I don't think I've ever seen more horribly broken piece of network software than Hero Siege and believe me, I've seen some seriously fucked up brain-damaged shit working as a professional and fairly low-level programmer and hobbyist gamedev. Out of morbid curiosity, I would like to peer into this abyss of shoddy sourcecode, knowingly that there could be an unspeakable, lovecraftian horror lurking inside, waiting for another soul to consume.

Think about everything that can go wrong with synchronising the state of two game clients (or rather: client and server) in a game like this and it will go wrong, plus a lot more. [b]Everything listed below (and more...) was observed while playing on LAN with wired Ethernet connection. No other active machines on network but a server and single client. There can be hardly an environment closer to perfection in multiplayer gaming, and still developers are bullcrapping people that the cause lies in lags and packet loss - see their posting from 8 Jan 2016.[/b]
[list]
[*] Monsters appearing out of nowhere and fucking you up? Check.
[*] Invisible ranged attacks (arrows, acid) from monsters fucking you up? You bet, check.
[*] Seeing traps in one place or state, while on the server they're somewhere else or in another state, therefore impaling you, smashing you around or otherwise fucking you up? Double fucking check.
[*] Seeing monsters in one place and attacking them, and seeing hits registering while in actuality they're somewhere else entirely and fucking you or someone else up? Oh my fucking Gaben...check!
[*] Not seeing special monster perks like "punisher" (spiky balls orbiting around monster, making melee attacks dangerous and usually fatal for the attacker) while you try to melee the undying shit out of that skeleton, unknowingly fucking yourself up? Kamikaze says: check.
[*] Not seeing pools of acid (map-based, not monster-attack-based) and similar stuff so that maneuvering in frantic combat can fuck you up out of the blue? Yep, check.
[*] Standing in place while the other game instance (server) sees you as shuffling a bit around, therefore potentially making you get hit with attack, that would otherwise not connect? Less dangerous, but still - check. Remember that server is the authority ([b]for now, read below...[/b]) on deciding which attack connects and which does not.
[*] Broken quests, where quest items don't spawn and quests are therefore unsolvable, but game registers them as done and you can get your reward instantly? Hm, this is actually rewarding and not punishing, but still a bug, so check please.
[*] [b]Seeing entirely different map from the server?[/b] You think I'm joking, right? That I'm smoking some unhealthy shit and seeing weird things. Tell you what - triple-down XXL motherfucking check with side order of fries. This was most easily reproduced in fight with V Act boss (Karp of Doom DLC).
[/list]

All of this was observed while playing side by side, so that I could compare in what state the server sees the world to what is displayed on the client by looking directly on neighboring computer screen.

What's really fun is that some of these problems are directly caused by game engine sucking big time on efficiency front and that networking is seemingly tied to the graphics engine, doing stuff like positions recalculations with each frame redraw. When FPS on server starts dropping for some reason (many monsters and items on the screen) while on the client FPS stays high, shit hits the fan in the most spectacular fashion. [b]Rule number two: you don't tie calculations of your world to how fast can you redraw this world on screen.[/b]

And don't get me started on playing on properly powerful machine. I comfortably played Diablo 2 (which looks better than Hero Siege BTW) on PentiumII 333 MHz. Fucking hell, even on 6-core 3.2 GHz CPU this game can noticeably lag while opening chests (when many coins are being spawned on screen) or starting another wave of monsters! We have GPUs for a reason, and that reason is not "standing idly while CPU works its ass off on graphics processing".

What's even more disconcerting is the current idea of dealing with the problems of desynchronisation. In news posting from 8 Jan 2016, developers stated that they want to move the responsibility of checking whether client was hit by a trap or a monster to the client itself.

Seriously. Let that thought sink in for a while.

[b]Rule number one: you do not trust the input from the client.[/b]

[b]Rule number zero: you DO NOT trust the input FROM THE CLIENT.[/b]

Or else you'll be having immortal players all around, faster than you'll be able to say "you are free to cheat as you like and we won't even bother checking shit".

To add insult to injury, developers are incompetent on the security front. They got hacked (cracked), not once but [b]twice[/b] and it resulted in mass banning of players by the crackers. I do not condone cracking, though it made me think about security practices applied in Panic Art Studios and whether they, for example, store players' passwords in plaintext. Though seeing how they want to fix problems with their networking by blindly believing input from clients, maybe I shouldn't be surprised.

Oh, did I mention that sometimes you'll spawn in town as another character class? E.g. you play a Pyromancer and someone else is Viking. Then sometimes when moving to town you'll become a Viking. Luckily this is only temporary but still it boggles the mind on how deep is the rabbit hole.

I think this game might be suffering from review bombers, or otherwise people just didn't know what they were buying.

[h1] Hero Siege	[/h1]

Hero Siege is a fun bullet hell game that is
similar to the Binding of Issac and has that nice rpg feel.

[h1] Graphics	[/h1]

As you can guess this game is pixelated like the olden times of games.

[h1] Gameplay	[/h1]

The gameplay for hero siege is massively enjoyable as a fun yet difficult twin stick shooter with a lot to offer. When you start off you will not have much at all but as you play the game you will recieve relics, equipment, and even potions, each adding to your abilities. The game has 7 base classes each with its own skill tree to discover and enjoy.

[h1] Singleplayer	[/h1] 

So far I have only had the chance to enjoy singleplayer and the necromancer class (so this review will focus on the necromancer class). The necromancer starts off with a skill tree where you can pick to have dead hands rise from the grave around you dealing damage or having the ability to summon 3 undead maruaders to your aid. As you level up you gain new points to invest in your skills with new tiers unlocking occassionally. The maps are somewhat randomly generated and contain traps that can damage both you and you enemies. Once you beat a certain # of enemies a boss will spawn. Sometimes the boss will be easy while others are much more difficult. Once you beat a boss a portal will open to continue to the next area and the boss will sometimes leave treasure chests and a relic for you to collect.

[h1] Relics/Chests	[/h1] 

ok so there are 3 types of chest you can find throughout the game.

[b] Wood Chest	[/b]
- as you can expect not that great loot but sometimes will drop a key

[b] Gold Chest	[/b]
- to open this chest you require a key and it wil usually have pretty decent items to find

[b] Crystal Chest	[/b]
-contains great loot and items to collect and require a crystal key to open

Ok now back to relics.
Relics are items you find in your game that can greatly help you. You gain relics after defeating a boss, buying from a shopkeeper or looting from a crypt/dungeon. There is an immense amount of relics that aid you throughout your journey from a hat that shoots out the symbol π at enemies to a fly swatter that does nothing but spawn a prop fly. There is an immense amount of relics so i recomment you check the wiki or the guide here on steam.

+ 7 classes with good possibilites
+ smooth gameplay with nice controls
+ i can summon the dead
+ pixelated and has nice rpg feel
+ equipment is useful
+ relics soooo many fun relics

[b] Cons	[/b]
- lagged immensly whenever i got an achievemt
- dlc a bit pricey

[h1] Final Thoughts	[/h1]

Hero siege is an amazing game with alot to offer. It has been a while since i have been able to enjoy a game like this. If you love the old pixelated rpg styles and love the binding of issac or bullet hell type games give Hero Siege a shot.

Brutally difficult dual-stick shooting done addictively right!

Two things first: 
1) This is a singleplayer review. If you're curious about multiplayer, read another review.
2) I didn't really care for Binding of Isaac, was moderately engaged by Hammerwatch, but mostly don't dabble in dual-stick shooters. What attracts me to this game is how it demands players to strive to a high level of skill while still maintaining the unforgiving difficulty that characterizes classic roguelikes. You're gonna die a lot and it's gonna suck, but the juice is worth the squeeze.
3) If you're bitching about not being able to shoot diagonally, I recommend you play a SNES game or two and suck it up, big boy.

PROS

- Wide variety of monsters and bosses, with nice touches of randomized customizations
- Surprisingly large selection of fully developed character classes
- One metric @#$%-ton of chievies (yeah, c'mon, nobody's going to play 150 hours)
- Sweet procedurally generated level designs with a delicious crunchy pixel-art style
- Loads of relics, potions, and blessings, with a well-integrated dungeon shop

CONS / Devs, please take note:

- Bosses are pretty uneven. Sometimes you'll get hulking brutes you can easily down, sometimes you'll get one-shotted instantly. Would be nice if they were a bit easier, but maybe it gets a bit more reasonable after leveling up a bit.
- PLEASE PUT IN A MINIMAP. I absolutely @#$%ing hate being chased around the map by the last monster of a wave just because I want to find that statue or dungeon that spawned. It's not a huge fix, won't break the game, and trust me, a lot of people will really appreciate it.


~~ Note for Roguelike Aficionados ~~
Stats and skills carry over after death (except temporary boosts, of which there are many varieties). I know what you're thinking, "Son, I am disappoint! I raised you to be a godlike 1337 rogue hardcore permadeath maximum difficulty pro, not some respawning filthy casul!" That's what I thought too, at first. Then after my 50th death without even getting to the second stage (and with a fair bit of skill, mind you!), I realized that I needed those XP levels to just... stick with me. You can probably guess that it does turn into a bit of a grind at that point, but that's where the game's charm kicks in.

Each character class has 4 unique abilities to learn and over twice as many passive skills. I tried the Viking and the Pirate, but ended up playing as a Pyromancer who I named "Solitary Eye". There is something distinctly gratifying about kiting around a bunch of high level monsters who could kill you in 3 or 4 hits and then igniting the ground around you in an enormous inferno while you spray jets of fire from your fingers at the largest beasts and summon meteors to crash down all around from the heavens... and they all die at once. You get XP, wade around in some blood, maybe grab a health orb if you're lucky (you won't need 'em though, you dangerous kiting expert, you), and pray for some of the more powerful basterds to drop keys.

Keys: keys are what you want. But be warned, having a bunch of keys and then finding no loot caves or chests to open, then getting merked by a stray lightning bolt you weren't paying attention to... that's gonna tick you off. A lot. Especially when you find 3 chests in your next play through and no keys. The loot dungeons, puzzle (and insanely dangerous) dungeons, and crypts filled with coins or crazy bosses... mayne, they're just really sexily implemented.

If you DO play the game in hardcore mode, you're probably Steven Hawking. Get a life.
